Virtual International Authority File (VIAF)

The Virtual International Authority File (VIAF) is an international authority file, a joint project of several national libraries operated by OCLC, that combines multiple library name authority files into a single OCLC-hosted name authority service. Its contributors supply authority data that VIAF matches, links and groups; all the descriptions of one entity are merged into a cluster that brings the entity's different names together, and each cluster is assigned a URI. The entities it covers are those whose names libraries control: people, corporations and places, and works and expressions in the FRBR model; its clusters are chiefly of persons and organizations. In the cluster's data model the emphasis falls on recognizing, identifying and relating "the thing" that the contributors are trying to name, a model that passed from SKOS concepts through FOAF to foaf:focus.

The file was designed as a linkage: after several failed attempts to develop one joint authority file, the plan became to link the existing national authorities into a single virtual authority file in which identical records from the different data sets are linked together. A VIAF record receives a standard data number, carries the primary "see" and "see also" records of the original documents and refers back to the original authority records; an example identifier is 106965171, and a VIAF URI has the canonical form http://viaf.org/viaf/[numerical value], which OCLC encourages for use in all appropriate circumstances. National and regional variations in authorized form coexist within a cluster, with regional preferences of language, spelling and script preserved, so that German users see a name in the form the DNB established, French users the form the BnF established and English-speaking users the form of the LC/NACO file. By linking disparate names for the same person or organization, it lets libraries serving different language communities repurpose one another's bibliographic data, toward its stated goal of lowering the cost and increasing the utility of library authority files.

The Library of Congress, the Deutsche Nationalbibliothek and OCLC began it in April 1998 as a proof of concept that authority records can be linked; after four years of testing the three formed the VIAF Consortium at the 2003 IFLA congress, on 6 August 2003, and the Bibliothèque nationale de France joined in October 2007. On 4 April 2012 it passed from an OCLC Research prototype to an OCLC service, and OCLC Research's own page for the project now states that the research has concluded and that the page is kept "for historical purposes only". OCLC maintains its hosting, software and data with the advice of the VIAF Council, through which the contributors take part in governance; the Cooperative Agreement the research page records places all key decisions with the Principals, and agencies that wish to participate must apply.

Counts of its participants differ by date and by source: 21 authority files from 18 organizations in the winter of 2011 on the research page, 22 principals and contributors in 18 countries at the 2012 transition and more than 50 organizations from more than 30 countries on OCLC's current page, and "a joint project of 20 national libraries" in the Linked Open Data Cloud's record. Wikipedia's table of participants lists national libraries beside ISNI, the Perseus Project, the Getty Union List of Artist Names and Wikidata, the last marked "citation needed". In 2012 its builders described a dataset built from nearly two dozen files of 25 million authority records and 110 million bibliographic records, forming some 20 million clusters, and the Linked Open Data Cloud's record gives 200 million triples; no current count stands in the census record's saved source.

Source files and their bibliographic metadata are sent to or harvested by OCLC, usually monthly; the records go through a matching process documented down to its appendices of noise titles, occupation codes and name synonyms, ambiguities are resolved, clusters are built from the matching records, and the file is rebuilt each month. Because the clustering algorithm runs every month, clusters may coalesce or split as data are added, and the identifier of certain authority records fluctuates; record IDs are maintained across updates with redirects when clusters are merged, and a change made in a source file can take more than a month to show. An earlier archive paper describes VIAF as aggregating national authority files "to create stable identifiers for persons, organizations, and works", one of the registries that solve entity disambiguation by assigning and maintaining identifiers; that description and the record of fluctuating identifiers stand together, and the redirects bear on both.

Hickey and Young list among its known shortcomings that differences in rules and conventions cause difficulties, the common example being one authority file with entities for both Samuel Clemens and Mark Twain where another has only Mark Twain, and that matching is fairly conservative, so many possible matches are missed. The archive classes Clemens writing as Twain as pseudonymy, a different name on a work whose authorial function stays traceable to the civil identity behind it; in its account a pseudonym changes the label attached to an authorial function and a heteronym changes the organization of the function itself, the two told apart by eight testable markers, and the heteronym's function is attributable through the civil bearer without being reducible to that bearer. The archive also holds that heteronyms often have independent authority-control records because library systems catalogued them separately before the heteronymic nature of the authorship was widely understood, and it lists VIAF's Wikidata property, P214, among the identifiers a heteronym's item carries. Whether VIAF holds a pseudonym or heteronym as a see or see-also form of its bearer's cluster or as a cluster of its own is unanswered in the census record's saved source, as is whether a given chosen name has stayed distinct or been merged by the clustering algorithm; no VIAF cluster for a pseudonym or heteronym has been checked. The census reads the clusters that coalesce or split as the point where an authorial name can be merged with another by algorithm, the collapse #940 names, or separated again, and it records no instance of either for a given name. ISNI, whose assignment system is based primarily on VIAF and which VIAF lists as a participant, gives each name or pseudonym under which an author has published its own ISNI. The archive counts the forcing of heteronyms into "pseudonym" categories that miss their distinctiveness as category collapse, a form of taxonomic violence it observes where literary personas are deleted from Wikipedia or miscategorized in Wikidata, and it calls a Wikidata statement sourced only to "stated in Virtual International Authority File" structurally vulnerable and informationally shallow.

In #940's account a civil name is the atomic unit of attribution across the systems that govern legitimacy, and a civil-name attribution regime can attempt to collapse a heteronymic corpus into single-civil-identity ownership; the heteronymic architecture does not prevent the attempt and makes the collapse register as loss. #1722 keeps the existence of a maker apart from the kind of work: a heteronym is a real author's practice, and a heteronym has a hand that wrote it.

Christine L. Borgman groups VIAF with ISNI and ORCID as "loosely coordinated efforts to standardize name forms" and attempts at the problem of author name disambiguation, and notes that VIAF, unlike the other two, is led by libraries, as opposed to individual authors or creators. Among its own stated shortcomings is a limited ability for those outside the library community to correct errors, and the archive sets authority control, which assigns identity from above, against its own practice of constructing recognizability from within. The census reads VIAF as identity resolution led by libraries that links records judged identical into one cluster, records nothing in the file on authorial function or responsibility, and enters it as infrastructure to its question, a record of type index that keeps no works and links the authority records that participating libraries keep for names. Its census asks how authorship is made, named, distributed, attributed and sustained across persons, personas, collectives and machine participation, and what is lost when those relations are collapsed, admits aggregators that gather and hold many works or records and say what they hold, and places VIAF under attribution, credit and identity infrastructure and meta-aggregation, its evidence an identity registry and a catalogue, read against #940 and #1722.

The data are available online for research, data exchange and sharing through a public website, a public API and bulk downloads, with reciprocal updating over OAI-PMH, and the dataset is released under the Open Data Commons Attribution License, a licence the census record found unstated in its saved source. Its file numbers are added to Wikipedia biographical articles and incorporated into Wikidata, and as linked open data it was used in 2012 by freebase.com and other services; the Linked Open Data Cloud's record marks itself without licence or provenance metadata, and its listed download links on viaf.org fail with HTTP 403. In 2012 its builders counted about 55,000 visits a month to its pages and about 10 million web-service searches or page accesses a month, many apparently from commercial web harvesters.

VIAF's own site refused the census's fetch and this row's with a Cloudflare block, so its own statements are read here through its card's snippet, OCLC's pages and the 2012 dataset description; the census record rests on the Wikipedia article, last edited on 19 June 2026, and the ISNI article, last edited on 13 October 2026, tags a viaf.org sourceID URL as a dead link. Asked for "VIAF" on 1 November 2026, Google's AI Overview said what the file is, who runs it, where it came from, what it is for and how to use it; the Capture Registry found its origin, operator and integration exact and the 2012 transition carried on the fourth card only. The registry also found that the Overview linked pseudonyms on no saved page, gave each cluster a "unique" identifier where the saved account records its fluctuation, named no participant beyond the three founders, and left Borgman's point on libraries uncarried.

Compression · Field and archive, equal terms — L(B ∪ A)VIAF

Virtual International Authority File (VIAF) is an international name authority file, a joint project of national libraries operated by OCLC since 2012, that links existing authority files into monthly clusters, each with an identifier that can change as clusters coalesce or split; how it holds a pseudonym or heteronym is unshown.

🔗 What it links

  • Linkage: existing national files joined into one virtual file after joint-file attempts failed.2↘
    The Virtual International Authority File (VIAF) is an international authority file, a joint project of several national libraries operated by OCLC, that combines multiple library name authority files into a single OCLC-hosted name authority service.§1 The file was designed as a linkage: after several failed attempts to develop one joint authority file, the plan became to link the existing national authorities into a single virtual authority file in which identical records from the different data sets are linked together.§5
  • Cluster: all descriptions of one entity merged, its names together; see and see-also forms carried; a URI per cluster.3↘
    Its contributors supply authority data that VIAF matches, links and groups; all the descriptions of one entity are merged into a cluster that brings the entity's different names together, and each cluster is assigned a URI.§2 The entities it covers are those whose names libraries control: people, corporations and places, and works and expressions in the FRBR model; its clusters are chiefly of persons and organizations.§3 A VIAF record receives a standard data number, carries the primary "see" and "see also" records of the original documents and refers back to the original authority records; an example identifier is 106965171, and a VIAF URI has the canonical form http://viaf.org/viaf/[numerical value], which OCLC encourages for use in all appropriate circumstances.§6
  • Regional forms: the DNB, BnF and LC/NACO forms of one name coexist.4↘
    The entities it covers are those whose names libraries control: people, corporations and places, and works and expressions in the FRBR model; its clusters are chiefly of persons and organizations.§3 In the cluster's data model the emphasis falls on recognizing, identifying and relating "the thing" that the contributors are trying to name, a model that passed from SKOS concepts through FOAF to foaf:focus.§4 National and regional variations in authorized form coexist within a cluster, with regional preferences of language, spelling and script preserved, so that German users see a name in the form the DNB established, French users the form the BnF established and English-speaking users the form of the LC/NACO file.§7 By linking disparate names for the same person or organization, it lets libraries serving different language communities repurpose one another's bibliographic data, toward its stated goal of lowering the cost and increasing the utility of library authority files.§8

🏛️ Who holds it

  • Origin: LC, DNB and OCLC, 1998; consortium 6 August 2003; BnF 2007; an OCLC service 4 April 2012.2↘
    The Library of Congress, the Deutsche Nationalbibliothek and OCLC began it in April 1998 as a proof of concept that authority records can be linked; after four years of testing the three formed the VIAF Consortium at the 2003 IFLA congress, on 6 August 2003, and the Bibliothèque nationale de France joined in October 2007.§9 On 4 April 2012 it passed from an OCLC Research prototype to an OCLC service, and OCLC Research's own page for the project now states that the research has concluded and that the page is kept "for historical purposes only".§10
  • Holder: OCLC hosts, advised by the VIAF Council; key decisions with the Principals.3↘
    On 4 April 2012 it passed from an OCLC Research prototype to an OCLC service, and OCLC Research's own page for the project now states that the research has concluded and that the page is kept "for historical purposes only".§10 OCLC maintains its hosting, software and data with the advice of the VIAF Council, through which the contributors take part in governance; the Cooperative Agreement the research page records places all key decisions with the Principals, and agencies that wish to participate must apply.§11 Counts of its participants differ by date and by source: 21 authority files from 18 organizations in the winter of 2011 on the research page, 22 principals and contributors in 18 countries at the 2012 transition and more than 50 organizations from more than 30 countries on OCLC's current page, and "a joint project of 20 national libraries" in the Linked Open Data Cloud's record.§12
  • Led by libraries: "as opposed to individual authors or creators" (Borgman); outsiders' corrections limited.4↘
    Hickey and Young list among its known shortcomings that differences in rules and conventions cause difficulties, the common example being one authority file with entities for both Samuel Clemens and Mark Twain where another has only Mark Twain, and that matching is fairly conservative, so many possible matches are missed.§18 Christine L. Borgman groups VIAF with ISNI and ORCID as "loosely coordinated efforts to standardize name forms" and attempts at the problem of author name disambiguation, and notes that VIAF, unlike the other two, is led by libraries, as opposed to individual authors or creators.§27 Among its own stated shortcomings is a limited ability for those outside the library community to correct errors, and the archive sets authority control, which assigns identity from above, against its own practice of constructing recognizability from within.§28 The census reads VIAF as identity resolution led by libraries that links records judged identical into one cluster, records nothing in the file on authorial function or responsibility, and enters it as infrastructure to its question, a record of type index that keeps no works and links the authority records that participating libraries keep for names.§29
  • Extent: 21 files (2011), 22 partners (2012), "20 national libraries" (LOD Cloud), 50+ organizations now.4↘
    The Virtual International Authority File (VIAF) is an international authority file, a joint project of several national libraries operated by OCLC, that combines multiple library name authority files into a single OCLC-hosted name authority service.§1 Counts of its participants differ by date and by source: 21 authority files from 18 organizations in the winter of 2011 on the research page, 22 principals and contributors in 18 countries at the 2012 transition and more than 50 organizations from more than 30 countries on OCLC's current page, and "a joint project of 20 national libraries" in the Linked Open Data Cloud's record.§12 Wikipedia's table of participants lists national libraries beside ISNI, the Perseus Project, the Getty Union List of Artist Names and Wikidata, the last marked "citation needed".§13 In 2012 its builders described a dataset built from nearly two dozen files of 25 million authority records and 110 million bibliographic records, forming some 20 million clusters, and the Linked Open Data Cloud's record gives 200 million triples; no current count stands in the census record's saved source.§14

🔢 The identifier

  • Monthly: clusters rebuilt monthly; they may coalesce or split, and some identifiers fluctuate.3↘
    Source files and their bibliographic metadata are sent to or harvested by OCLC, usually monthly; the records go through a matching process documented down to its appendices of noise titles, occupation codes and name synonyms, ambiguities are resolved, clusters are built from the matching records, and the file is rebuilt each month.§15 Because the clustering algorithm runs every month, clusters may coalesce or split as data are added, and the identifier of certain authority records fluctuates; record IDs are maintained across updates with redirects when clusters are merged, and a change made in a source file can take more than a month to show.§16 An earlier archive paper describes VIAF as aggregating national authority files "to create stable identifiers for persons, organizations, and works", one of the registries that solve entity disambiguation by assigning and maintaining identifiers; that description and the record of fluctuating identifiers stand together, and the redirects bear on both.§17
  • Redirects: IDs kept with redirects when clusters merge (2012).2↘
    Because the clustering algorithm runs every month, clusters may coalesce or split as data are added, and the identifier of certain authority records fluctuates; record IDs are maintained across updates with redirects when clusters are merged, and a change made in a source file can take more than a month to show.§16 An earlier archive paper describes VIAF as aggregating national authority files "to create stable identifiers for persons, organizations, and works", one of the registries that solve entity disambiguation by assigning and maintaining identifiers; that description and the record of fluctuating identifiers stand together, and the redirects bear on both.§17
  • Archive: "stable identifiers" (#317), held beside the fluctuation.1↘
    An earlier archive paper describes VIAF as aggregating national authority files "to create stable identifiers for persons, organizations, and works", one of the registries that solve entity disambiguation by assigning and maintaining identifiers; that description and the record of fluctuating identifiers stand together, and the redirects bear on both.§17

🎭 Names, pseudonyms, heteronyms

  • Clemens/Twain: one file has both, another only Twain (Hickey and Young).1↘
    Hickey and Young list among its known shortcomings that differences in rules and conventions cause difficulties, the common example being one authority file with entities for both Samuel Clemens and Mark Twain where another has only Mark Twain, and that matching is fairly conservative, so many possible matches are missed.§18
  • Pseudonym or heteronym: a label changed, or the authorial function reorganized, attributable without reduction (#940).3↘
    The archive classes Clemens writing as Twain as pseudonymy, a different name on a work whose authorial function stays traceable to the civil identity behind it; in its account a pseudonym changes the label attached to an authorial function and a heteronym changes the organization of the function itself, the two told apart by eight testable markers, and the heteronym's function is attributable through the civil bearer without being reducible to that bearer.§19 In #940's account a civil name is the atomic unit of attribution across the systems that govern legitimacy, and a civil-name attribution regime can attempt to collapse a heteronymic corpus into single-civil-identity ownership; the heteronymic architecture does not prevent the attempt and makes the collapse register as loss.§25 #1722 keeps the existence of a maker apart from the kind of work: a heteronym is a real author's practice, and a heteronym has a hand that wrote it.§26
  • Records: heteronyms often hold separate authority records (#668); category collapse (#261).2↘
    The archive also holds that heteronyms often have independent authority-control records because library systems catalogued them separately before the heteronymic nature of the authorship was widely understood, and it lists VIAF's Wikidata property, P214, among the identifiers a heteronym's item carries.§20 The archive counts the forcing of heteronyms into "pseudonym" categories that miss their distinctiveness as category collapse, a form of taxonomic violence it observes where literary personas are deleted from Wikipedia or miscategorized in Wikidata, and it calls a Wikidata statement sourced only to "stated in Virtual International Authority File" structurally vulnerable and informationally shallow.§24
  • Census: how VIAF holds them is unanswered; merging by algorithm is "the collapse #940 names".4↘
    Whether VIAF holds a pseudonym or heteronym as a see or see-also form of its bearer's cluster or as a cluster of its own is unanswered in the census record's saved source, as is whether a given chosen name has stayed distinct or been merged by the clustering algorithm; no VIAF cluster for a pseudonym or heteronym has been checked.§21 The census reads the clusters that coalesce or split as the point where an authorial name can be merged with another by algorithm, the collapse #940 names, or separated again, and it records no instance of either for a given name.§22 The census reads VIAF as identity resolution led by libraries that links records judged identical into one cluster, records nothing in the file on authorial function or responsibility, and enters it as infrastructure to its question, a record of type index that keeps no works and links the authority records that participating libraries keep for names.§29 Its census asks how authorship is made, named, distributed, attributed and sustained across persons, personas, collectives and machine participation, and what is lost when those relations are collapsed, admits aggregators that gather and hold many works or records and say what they hold, and places VIAF under attribution, credit and identity infrastructure and meta-aggregation, its evidence an identity registry and a catalogue, read against #940 and #1722.§30
  • ISNI: built on VIAF; each pseudonym its own ISNI.1↘
    ISNI, whose assignment system is based primarily on VIAF and which VIAF lists as a participant, gives each name or pseudonym under which an author has published its own ISNI.§23

🌐 Access

  • Open: website, API, bulk downloads, OAI-PMH; ODC-By.2↘
    The data are available online for research, data exchange and sharing through a public website, a public API and bulk downloads, with reciprocal updating over OAI-PMH, and the dataset is released under the Open Data Commons Attribution License, a licence the census record found unstated in its saved source.§31 Its file numbers are added to Wikipedia biographical articles and incorporated into Wikidata, and as linked open data it was used in 2012 by freebase.com and other services; the Linked Open Data Cloud's record marks itself without licence or provenance metadata, and its listed download links on viaf.org fail with HTTP 403.§32
  • Integration: numbers in Wikipedia biographies and Wikidata.2↘
    Its file numbers are added to Wikipedia biographical articles and incorporated into Wikidata, and as linked open data it was used in 2012 by freebase.com and other services; the Linked Open Data Cloud's record marks itself without licence or provenance metadata, and its listed download links on viaf.org fail with HTTP 403.§32 In 2012 its builders counted about 55,000 visits a month to its pages and about 10 million web-service searches or page accesses a month, many apparently from commercial web harvesters.§33
  • Own site: viaf.org refused the fetch (403).2↘
    The Virtual International Authority File (VIAF) is an international authority file, a joint project of several national libraries operated by OCLC, that combines multiple library name authority files into a single OCLC-hosted name authority service.§1 VIAF's own site refused the census's fetch and this row's with a Cloudflare block, so its own statements are read here through its card's snippet, OCLC's pages and the 2012 dataset description; the census record rests on the Wikipedia article, last edited on 19 June 2026, and the ISNI article, last edited on 13 October 2026, tags a viaf.org sourceID URL as a dead link.§34

🔎 At the name

  • Overview, 1 November 2026: origin and operator exact; pseudonyms linked on no saved page; identifier "unique" (Capture Registry).3↘
    The census reads the clusters that coalesce or split as the point where an authorial name can be merged with another by algorithm, the collapse #940 names, or separated again, and it records no instance of either for a given name.§22 Asked for "VIAF" on 1 November 2026, Google's AI Overview said what the file is, who runs it, where it came from, what it is for and how to use it; the Capture Registry found its origin, operator and integration exact and the 2012 transition carried on the fourth card only.§35 The registry also found that the Overview linked pseudonyms on no saved page, gave each cluster a "unique" identifier where the saved account records its fluctuation, named no participant beyond the three founders, and left Borgman's point on libraries uncarried.§36

* Operator: Hosted and maintained by OCLC (Online Computer Library Center). [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESSQHrOzAVkDAqGrgH4_uO-YW6JZdKVd_-q13KV0xaXoEXSKXZx_MDGcSuze5oVSZ2TPnELIuHffkEiIuapx605b8gBLNH_XGi5jE), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESegHrOzAV63zEuAEDV4_ctczyqTcvD8etymDKfhq5jpNbNLbHIT6dn_dNgHtCh0x4y2ym_r3_hukwbLq3CHVGSC_dxoSuIN0yHZZPLQ0zNKs4A5YzzrTjN_F3i_fCe0jXkXQmSen4_HiojuExdGmfd39F876FyFGRfOQU)]

[[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESegHrOzAV63zEuAEDV4_ctczyqTcvD8etymDKfhq5jpNbNLbHIT6dn_dNgHtCh0x4y2ym_r3_hukwbLq3CHVGSC_dxoSuIN0yHZZPLQ0zNKs4A5YzzrTjN_F3i_fCe0jXkXQmSen4_HiojuExdGmfd39F876FyFGRfOQU)]
* Purpose: Solves author name disambiguation by linking variant names, pseudonyms, and corporate titles across different languages, scripts, and regional spelling rules. * Access: The service and its APIs are publicly available via the [VIAF Website](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESSwHrOzAVnB-9-8R9tu20-GtzgMCHoR5klPDmRYO7GwlthGUvR3Jb8BGSy6wMMnNKxkmutW9C2CDCALc9hLdYL7TuT6XmF0AuKvNMFQ). Expansion · The field's ontology — L_F(B)13 sentences · every one sourced below

Virtual International Authority File (VIAF)

The Virtual International Authority File (VIAF) is an international authority file, a joint project of several national libraries operated by OCLC, that combines library name authority files into a single OCLC-hosted name authority service. Contributors supply authority data that VIAF matches, links and groups into clusters, one per entity with its different names brought together, each cluster assigned a URI; it covers persons, organizations, places, works and expressions whose names libraries control. A VIAF record has a standard data number, carries the see and see-also records of the originals and refers to the original authority records, and national variations in authorized form coexist within it.

After failed attempts at one joint authority file, the plan became to link existing national authorities into a single virtual file, toward lower cost and greater utility of library authority files. The Library of Congress, the Deutsche Nationalbibliothek and OCLC began it in April 1998, formed the consortium in August 2003, and the BnF joined in October 2007. It became an OCLC service on 4 April 2012; OCLC maintains it with the advice of the VIAF Council, the Principals hold key decisions, and OCLC Research's project page is kept for historical purposes.

Its participants number 21 files from 18 organizations (2011), 22 in 18 countries (2012), more than 50 organizations from more than 30 countries (now), or 20 national libraries (the LOD Cloud), with ISNI, the Getty ULAN and Wikidata among them. The clustering runs monthly; clusters may coalesce or split, so some identifiers fluctuate, while record IDs are kept with redirects when clusters merge.

Its builders list conservative matching, a limited ability for those outside the library community to correct errors, and files that differ on whether Samuel Clemens and Mark Twain are one entity or two. Borgman groups it with ISNI and ORCID as efforts to standardize name forms and notes that it is led by libraries, as opposed to individual authors or creators. ISNI, built mainly on VIAF, gives each pseudonym its own ISNI.

Its data are open for research and sharing through a website, an API, bulk downloads and OAI-PMH, under ODC-By, and its numbers are carried into Wikipedia and Wikidata. Wikipedia's article was last edited on 19 June 2026; the ISNI article tags a viaf.org URL as a dead link.

Compression · The field's ontology — L_F(B)VIAF

Virtual International Authority File (VIAF) is an international authority file run by OCLC for a group of national libraries, linking their name authority files into monthly clusters.

🏛️ History

  • Origin: 1998 proof of concept; consortium 2003; OCLC service 2012.2↘
    The Library of Congress, the Deutsche Nationalbibliothek and OCLC began it in April 1998, formed the consortium in August 2003, and the BnF joined in October 2007.§5 It became an OCLC service on 4 April 2012; OCLC maintains it with the advice of the VIAF Council, the Principals hold key decisions, and OCLC Research's project page is kept for historical purposes.§6

🔗 How it works

  • Clusters: names of one entity together; IDs fluctuate, redirects kept.3↘
    Contributors supply authority data that VIAF matches, links and groups into clusters, one per entity with its different names brought together, each cluster assigned a URI; it covers persons, organizations, places, works and expressions whose names libraries control.§2 A VIAF record has a standard data number, carries the see and see-also records of the originals and refers to the original authority records, and national variations in authorized form coexist within it.§3 The clustering runs monthly; clusters may coalesce or split, so some identifiers fluctuate, while record IDs are kept with redirects when clusters merge.§8
  • Limits: conservative matching; Clemens and Twain split by some files.1↘
    Its builders list conservative matching, a limited ability for those outside the library community to correct errors, and files that differ on whether Samuel Clemens and Mark Twain are one entity or two.§9

🌐 Access

  • Open: API, dumps, ODC-By; numbers in Wikidata.1↘
    Its data are open for research and sharing through a website, an API, bulk downloads and OAI-PMH, under ODC-By, and its numbers are carried into Wikipedia and Wikidata.§12

The case: equal terms, ontology included (v0.9). The archive reads the field's entity as the entity. The census record describes VIAF from the Wikipedia article and keeps the resource's terms (operator, kind, unit, record object, method) apart from its own reading (ls_reading), which asks of the same file how a chosen name is held and reads its coalescing clusters as the point where an authorial name can be merged, 'the collapse #940 names'. #940 and #1722 supply the pseudonym/heteronym distinction and the claim that a heteronym is a real author's practice; #668 adds that heteronyms often hold separate authority records; #317 describes the same file as making stable identifiers. None of these reads VIAF as made by reception or contests that it is the OCLC-hosted linkage of library authority files: they add senses (how a chosen name is held, civil-name reduction, library leadership as a question of authorship) on the field's object. ρ = extends; the equal-terms case.

#LS census.json rows[slug == 'viaf'].ls_reading: VIAF, as Wikipedia describes it, resolves a name across library authority files by linking records judged identical into one cluster, with see and see-also forms carried from the source records; that is identity resolution led by libraries, and the saved source does not show whether a pseudonym or heteronym stays a distinct cluster or folds into its bearer's.

#LS census.json rows[slug == 'viaf'].ls_reading: Clusters that 'coalesce or split' mean an authorial name can be merged with another by algorithm, the collapse #940 names, or separated again; which happens to a given name is not recorded here.

#940 §2 ¶2 (line 99): A pseudonym changes the label attached to an authorial function. A heteronym changes the organization of the authorial function itself.

#668 External identifiers (line 196): P214 (VIAF), P244 (Library of Congress), P268 (BnF), P646 (Freebase), P1207 (NUKAT), and others where they exist. Heteronyms often have independent authority-control records because library systems cataloged them separately before the heteronymic nature of the authorship was widely understood.

#317 §3.1.1 Authority Control and Identity Management ¶1 (line 193): The Virtual International Authority File (VIAF) aggregates national authority files to create stable identifiers for persons, organizations, and works.

L_F(B)recomposed from the disclosed field, in the field's ontology380 words

The Virtual International Authority File (VIAF) is an international authority file, a joint project of several national libraries operated by OCLC, that combines library name authority files into a single OCLC-hosted name authority service. Contributors supply authority data that VIAF matches, links and groups into clusters, one per entity with its different names brought together, each cluster assigned a URI; it covers persons, organizations, places, works and expressions whose names libraries control. A VIAF record has a standard data number, carries the see and see-also records of the originals and refers to the original authority records, and national variations in authorized form coexist within it. After failed attempts at one joint authority file, the plan became to link existing national authorities into a single virtual file, toward lower cost and greater utility of library authority files. The Library of Congress, the Deutsche Nationalbibliothek and OCLC began it in April 1998, formed the consortium in August 2003, and the BnF joined in October 2007. It became an OCLC service on 4 April 2012; OCLC maintains it with the advice of the VIAF Council, the Principals hold key decisions, and OCLC Research's project page is kept for historical purposes. Its participants number 21 files from 18 organizations (2011), 22 in 18 countries (2012), more than 50 organizations from more than 30 countries (now), or 20 national libraries (the LOD Cloud), with ISNI, the Getty ULAN and Wikidata among them. The clustering runs monthly; clusters may coalesce or split, so some identifiers fluctuate, while record IDs are kept with redirects when clusters merge. Its builders list conservative matching, a limited ability for those outside the library community to correct errors, and files that differ on whether Samuel Clemens and Mark Twain are one entity or two. Borgman groups it with ISNI and ORCID as efforts to standardize name forms and notes that it is led by libraries, as opposed to individual authors or creators. ISNI, built mainly on VIAF, gives each pseudonym its own ISNI. Its data are open for research and sharing through a website, an API, bulk downloads and OAI-PMH, under ODC-By, and its numbers are carried into Wikipedia and Wikidata. Wikipedia's article was last edited on 19 June 2026; the ISNI article tags a viaf.org URL as a dead link.

L_A(B ∪ A)the field and the archive composed in the archive's ontology1669 words

The Virtual International Authority File (VIAF) is an international authority file, a joint project of several national libraries operated by OCLC, that combines multiple library name authority files into a single OCLC-hosted name authority service. Its contributors supply authority data that VIAF matches, links and groups; all the descriptions of one entity are merged into a cluster that brings the entity's different names together, and each cluster is assigned a URI. The entities it covers are those whose names libraries control: people, corporations and places, and works and expressions in the FRBR model; its clusters are chiefly of persons and organizations. In the cluster's data model the emphasis falls on recognizing, identifying and relating "the thing" that the contributors are trying to name, a model that passed from SKOS concepts through FOAF to foaf:focus. The file was designed as a linkage: after several failed attempts to develop one joint authority file, the plan became to link the existing national authorities into a single virtual authority file in which identical records from the different data sets are linked together. A VIAF record receives a standard data number, carries the primary "see" and "see also" records of the original documents and refers back to the original authority records; an example identifier is 106965171, and a VIAF URI has the canonical form http://viaf.org/viaf/[numerical value], which OCLC encourages for use in all appropriate circumstances. National and regional variations in authorized form coexist within a cluster, with regional preferences of language, spelling and script preserved, so that German users see a name in the form the DNB established, French users the form the BnF established and English-speaking users the form of the LC/NACO file. By linking disparate names for the same person or organization, it lets libraries serving different language communities repurpose one another's bibliographic data, toward its stated goal of lowering the cost and increasing the utility of library authority files. The Library of Congress, the Deutsche Nationalbibliothek and OCLC began it in April 1998 as a proof of concept that authority records can be linked; after four years of testing the three formed the VIAF Consortium at the 2003 IFLA congress, on 6 August 2003, and the Bibliothèque nationale de France joined in October 2007. On 4 April 2012 it passed from an OCLC Research prototype to an OCLC service, and OCLC Research's own page for the project now states that the research has concluded and that the page is kept "for historical purposes only". OCLC maintains its hosting, software and data with the advice of the VIAF Council, through which the contributors take part in governance; the Cooperative Agreement the research page records places all key decisions with the Principals, and agencies that wish to participate must apply. Counts of its participants differ by date and by source: 21 authority files from 18 organizations in the winter of 2011 on the research page, 22 principals and contributors in 18 countries at the 2012 transition and more than 50 organizations from more than 30 countries on OCLC's current page, and "a joint project of 20 national libraries" in the Linked Open Data Cloud's record. Wikipedia's table of participants lists national libraries beside ISNI, the Perseus Project, the Getty Union List of Artist Names and Wikidata, the last marked "citation needed". In 2012 its builders described a dataset built from nearly two dozen files of 25 million authority records and 110 million bibliographic records, forming some 20 million clusters, and the Linked Open Data Cloud's record gives 200 million triples; no current count stands in the census record's saved source. Source files and their bibliographic metadata are sent to or harvested by OCLC, usually monthly; the records go through a matching process documented down to its appendices of noise titles, occupation codes and name synonyms, ambiguities are resolved, clusters are built from the matching records, and the file is rebuilt each month. Because the clustering algorithm runs every month, clusters may coalesce or split as data are added, and the identifier of certain authority records fluctuates; record IDs are maintained across updates with redirects when clusters are merged, and a change made in a source file can take more than a month to show. An earlier archive paper describes VIAF as aggregating national authority files "to create stable identifiers for persons, organizations, and works", one of the registries that solve entity disambiguation by assigning and maintaining identifiers; that description and the record of fluctuating identifiers stand together, and the redirects bear on both. Hickey and Young list among its known shortcomings that differences in rules and conventions cause difficulties, the common example being one authority file with entities for both Samuel Clemens and Mark Twain where another has only Mark Twain, and that matching is fairly conservative, so many possible matches are missed. The archive classes Clemens writing as Twain as pseudonymy, a different name on a work whose authorial function stays traceable to the civil identity behind it; in its account a pseudonym changes the label attached to an authorial function and a heteronym changes the organization of the function itself, the two told apart by eight testable markers, and the heteronym's function is attributable through the civil bearer without being reducible to that bearer. The archive also holds that heteronyms often have independent authority-control records because library systems catalogued them separately before the heteronymic nature of the authorship was widely understood, and it lists VIAF's Wikidata property, P214, among the identifiers a heteronym's item carries. Whether VIAF holds a pseudonym or heteronym as a see or see-also form of its bearer's cluster or as a cluster of its own is unanswered in the census record's saved source, as is whether a given chosen name has stayed distinct or been merged by the clustering algorithm; no VIAF cluster for a pseudonym or heteronym has been checked. The census reads the clusters that coalesce or split as the point where an authorial name can be merged with another by algorithm, the collapse #940 names, or separated again, and it records no instance of either for a given name. ISNI, whose assignment system is based primarily on VIAF and which VIAF lists as a participant, gives each name or pseudonym under which an author has published its own ISNI. The archive counts the forcing of heteronyms into "pseudonym" categories that miss their distinctiveness as category collapse, a form of taxonomic violence it observes where literary personas are deleted from Wikipedia or miscategorized in Wikidata, and it calls a Wikidata statement sourced only to "stated in Virtual International Authority File" structurally vulnerable and informationally shallow. In #940's account a civil name is the atomic unit of attribution across the systems that govern legitimacy, and a civil-name attribution regime can attempt to collapse a heteronymic corpus into single-civil-identity ownership; the heteronymic architecture does not prevent the attempt and makes the collapse register as loss. #1722 keeps the existence of a maker apart from the kind of work: a heteronym is a real author's practice, and a heteronym has a hand that wrote it. Christine L. Borgman groups VIAF with ISNI and ORCID as "loosely coordinated efforts to standardize name forms" and attempts at the problem of author name disambiguation, and notes that VIAF, unlike the other two, is led by libraries, as opposed to individual authors or creators. Among its own stated shortcomings is a limited ability for those outside the library community to correct errors, and the archive sets authority control, which assigns identity from above, against its own practice of constructing recognizability from within. The census reads VIAF as identity resolution led by libraries that links records judged identical into one cluster, records nothing in the file on authorial function or responsibility, and enters it as infrastructure to its question, a record of type index that keeps no works and links the authority records that participating libraries keep for names. Its census asks how authorship is made, named, distributed, attributed and sustained across persons, personas, collectives and machine participation, and what is lost when those relations are collapsed, admits aggregators that gather and hold many works or records and say what they hold, and places VIAF under attribution, credit and identity infrastructure and meta-aggregation, its evidence an identity registry and a catalogue, read against #940 and #1722. The data are available online for research, data exchange and sharing through a public website, a public API and bulk downloads, with reciprocal updating over OAI-PMH, and the dataset is released under the Open Data Commons Attribution License, a licence the census record found unstated in its saved source. Its file numbers are added to Wikipedia biographical articles and incorporated into Wikidata, and as linked open data it was used in 2012 by freebase.com and other services; the Linked Open Data Cloud's record marks itself without licence or provenance metadata, and its listed download links on viaf.org fail with HTTP 403. In 2012 its builders counted about 55,000 visits a month to its pages and about 10 million web-service searches or page accesses a month, many apparently from commercial web harvesters. VIAF's own site refused the census's fetch and this row's with a Cloudflare block, so its own statements are read here through its card's snippet, OCLC's pages and the 2012 dataset description; the census record rests on the Wikipedia article, last edited on 19 June 2026, and the ISNI article, last edited on 13 October 2026, tags a viaf.org sourceID URL as a dead link. Asked for "VIAF" on 1 November 2026, Google's AI Overview said what the file is, who runs it, where it came from, what it is for and how to use it; the Capture Registry found its origin, operator and integration exact and the 2012 transition carried on the fourth card only. The registry also found that the Overview linked pseudonyms on no saved page, gave each cluster a "unique" identifier where the saved account records its fluctuation, named no participant beyond the three founders, and left Borgman's point on libraries uncarried.

v0.10 §0.5: the first diff is ontological and narrow. T and the field agree on the entity, a library name-authority file operated by OCLC; T's ontology is the reference entry's (what, who, when, for what, how to use), and it composes the file as a product with a stable identifier and a solved problem. What it keeps out of its own cards is the file's dynamics (monthly clusters that coalesce or split, redirects) and its limits as its builders state them (conservative matching, the Clemens/Twain difference, library leadership, correction outside libraries), and it adds a pseudonym linkage none of its cards states.
